lesson.title: Service books and the liturgical cycle

readings.title: Service Book
readings.text: (i) The Slushibnik, or Service Book, which contains most of the fixed portions of the Liturgies of St. John Chrysostom and St. Basil the Great, and of the Presanctified Gifts ; also the Litanies and Prayers of Vespers and Matins, together with the Graduals and Benedictions appropriate to all occasions. This is used by the Priest and the Choir.

readings.title: Canon and Scripture
readings.text: (10) As joy expresses itself in song, so the holy Church has appointed to be sung, after the salutation of the Book of the Gospels, the Nine Songs of the Canon, which represent the Hymns of praise, at the Resurrection, of the nine Ranks of the heavenly Hierarchy. The Canon contains, also, the Hymns of those godly persons in the Old Testament, from Moses to Zacharias, who magnified the Lord God in spiritual songs. This is in conformity with the teachings of our Lord himself, who, after his Resurrection, expounded unto his Disciples the things in all the Scriptures concerning himself; and each Song (Irmós), in the vast number of Canons in the Holy Orthodox Church, is inspired by the Hymn of Scripture appointed to precede it. But these Scripture hymns are generally omitted, with the exception of the Song of the Holy Birth-giver of God, which precedes Song IX.

scripture.translation: King James Version (public domain in the United States)
scripture.text:
O come, let us sing unto the Lord: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation.

Let us come before his presence with thanksgiving, and make a joyful noise unto him with psalms.

For the Lord is a great God, and a great King above all gods.

In his hand are the deep places of the earth: the strength of the hills is his also.

The sea is his, and he made it: and his hands formed the dry land.

O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the Lord our maker.

For he is our God; and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand. To day if ye will hear his voice,

overview.text: Orthodox services draw their texts from different books and hymn collections. The Service Book contains fixed portions used across services, while the canon is a structured series of hymns discussed in the Matins explanation. The same word canon has other meanings elsewhere; here it refers to hymnography.
overview.reason: The owner authorized a plain-English curriculum explanation so beginners can understand the topic before consulting the preserved source passage.

readings.title: What is in the Service Book?

paragraphs.text: Hapgood identifies the Service Book as containing fixed material for the Liturgies of John Chrysostom, Basil, and the Presanctified Gifts. It also contains litanies and prayers for Vespers and Matins. The description explains why a single book contains material for more than one service.

readings.title: What does canon mean in a service?

paragraphs.text: Here a canon is a sequence of songs connected with biblical hymns. Hapgood relates the sequence to the praise of figures in Scripture and to the interpretation of Scripture through Christ. She also distinguishes the biblical songs that supply the pattern from their customary omission in the service practice she describes.
